label: L20a
title: Interpretable Clustering
brief: Clustering is unsupervised: it segments data into groups of similar observations without labels, for market segmentation, document clustering, image regions, or as a first step before fitting one predictive model per group. Because the true partition is unknown, the result depends on the distance metric (Euclidean, Manhattan, Chebyshev, or the general Minkowski family), the algorithm and the quality criterion. Partition algorithms such as K-means start from a random assignment and alternate between assigning points to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids; hierarchical agglomerative clustering starts from singletons and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters under a chosen linkage (complete, single, average or centroid), giving a deterministic dendrogram that can be cut at any K. Neither output is interpretable, so the lecture's idea is to run K-means, label each point with its cluster, and fit an Optimal Classification Tree with K classes whose splits describe the clusters. On 79,593 Blue Bikes (Hubway) rides described by duration, gender and day of week, this yields readable segments such as female commuters, male commuters, weekend riders, short rides and, at K = 5, long rides.
kp: Clustering is unsupervised: it needs data but no labels, and aims to segment rather than predict.
Applications: market segmentation, document clustering, regions of images, and as an initial step before building a predictive model per group.
With no ground truth, the partition depends on (1) the distance metric, (2) the algorithm, (3) the criterion used to judge quality.

Distances: Euclidean $\sqrt{\sum_k (x_{ik}-x_{jk})^2}$, Manhattan $\sum_k |x_{ik}-x_{jk}|$, Chebyshev $\max_k |x_{ik}-x_{jk}|$; Minkowski generalizes them ($p=1$ Manhattan, $p=2$ Euclidean, $p\to\infty$ Chebyshev).
Partition (flat) algorithms: K-means, mixture of Gaussians, spectral clustering, which start random and refine. Hierarchical: agglomerative (bottom-up) or divisive (top-down), deterministic.
K-means: choose K, assign points, compute centroids, reassign each point to its closest centroid, recompute, repeat until no improvement.

Agglomerative clustering: start with every point in its own cluster and merge the two nearest clusters until one remains; linkage defines cluster distance: complete (max), single (min), average (mean), centroid.
Dendrogram: vertical line heights are the distances at which clusters merge; a horizontal cut picks the number of clusters.
K-means: low memory, sensitive to initialization, K fixed in advance. Hierarchical: more computation, deterministic, shows partitions for every K. Neither is interpretable.
Interpretable clustering: run K-means, label points by cluster, train an OCT with K classes; on Blue Bikes this gives segments like female/male commuters, weekend riders, short rides and long rides.

topics.x: Clustering groups similar instances without labels, for segmentation tasks or as a pre-step to per-group predictive models. Since the true partition is unknown, the same data can be partitioned in many ways depending on the metric, algorithm and evaluation criterion.

Euclidean distance is the root of summed squared coordinate differences, Manhattan the sum of absolute differences, and Chebyshev the largest absolute difference. Minkowski distance with parameter $p$ generalizes them: $p=1$ is Manhattan, $p=2$ Euclidean and $p\to\infty$ Chebyshev.

A partition algorithm that fixes K, starts from a random assignment and alternates two steps: assign each point to the nearest centroid and recompute each centroid as the mean of its points. It uses little memory but depends on the random start.

Agglomerative clustering begins with singletons and keeps merging the two nearest clusters, where cluster distance is set by the linkage: complete, single, average or centroid. The dendrogram records merge heights and lets the user choose K by a horizontal cut; it is deterministic but more computationally intensive than K-means.

Neither K-means nor hierarchical clustering gives features that characterize each cluster. Running K-means, labeling points by cluster and fitting an Optimal Classification Tree with K classes produces splits on the original features that describe each cluster.

2011 Hubway data, 79,593 rides after dropping missing records, with ride duration, rider gender and day of week. As K grows from 2 to 5 the OCT leaves become interpretable segments: female commuters, male commuters, weekend riders, short rides and long rides; several leaves can map to the same cluster.

cards.b: The goal is to segment the data into similar groups rather than predict; it needs data but no labels.
cards.x: Without labels there is no ground-truth partition to score against.

cards.f: Four applications of clustering named in the lecture.
cards.b: Market segmentation; document clustering; regions of images; an initial step for a predictive model (cluster into similar groups, then build a model per group).
cards.x: The last one links clustering to supervised learning.

cards.f: Three choices that determine how a data set gets partitioned.
cards.b: (1) The distance metric used for pairwise similarity. (2) The algorithm used to partition the space. (3) The criterion used to assess the quality of the solution.
cards.x: Change any one and the 'right' clusters can change.

cards.b: Chebyshev: $d(i,j) = \max_k |x_{ik}-x_{jk}|$. Minkowski generalizes: $d(i,j) = (\sum_k |x_{ik}-x_{jk}|^p)^{1/p}$; $p=1$ gives Manhattan, $p=2$ Euclidean, $p\to\infty$ Chebyshev.
cards.x: Chebyshev only looks at the single largest coordinate gap.

cards.b: Partition algorithms start from a random (partial) partition and refine it iteratively: K-means, mixture of Gaussians, spectral clustering. Hierarchical algorithms give a deterministic solution: bottom-up agglomerative or top-down divisive.
cards.x: Randomness vs determinism is the key split.

cards.f: Steps of the K-means algorithm (lecture example).
cards.b: (1) Specify K. (2) Randomly assign each point to a cluster. (3) Compute cluster centroids. (4) Reassign each point to the closest centroid. (5) Recompute centroids. (6) Repeat 4-5 until no improvement.
Start with each data point in its own cluster; combine the two nearest clusters; keep combining the next two nearest until all observations are in one cluster.
cards.x: No K needed up front; the full merge history is kept.

cards.f: Four linkage types between clusters A and B.
cards.b: Complete: maximum pairwise distance. Single: minimum pairwise distance. Average: mean pairwise distance. Centroid: distance between the two centroids.
cards.x: Linkage is what hierarchical clustering needs that K-means does not: a distance between clusters.

cards.f: How do you read a dendrogram?
cards.b: Data points are listed along the bottom; the height of each vertical line is the distance between the clusters being merged. Any horizontal cut defines a number of clusters.
cards.x: Cut where there is a long vertical gap to get well-separated clusters.

cards.b: K-means: low memory, results sensitive to random initialization, K pre-defined. Hierarchical: more computationally intensive, deterministic, dendrogram suggests partitions for many K. Both: results are not interpretable.
cards.x: Neither tells you which features characterize a cluster.

cards.f: The lecture's recipe for interpretable clustering.
cards.b: Run K-means; label each point with its cluster; train an Optimal Classification Tree with K classes on the features. The tree's splits interpret the clusters.
cards.x: The OCT turns an unsupervised result into a supervised, readable one.

cards.f: Blue Bikes data used in the case study.
cards.b: 2011 Hubway ridership, 79,593 rides after removing records with missing values; variables: ride duration (minutes), rider gender, day of week (1-7).
cards.x: Only three features, so tree rules stay short.

cards.f: The four Blue Bikes clusters and their interpretation.
cards.b: Female commuters (female weekday rides over 4 min); weekend riders (weekend rides over 4-5 min); short rides (under 4-8 min); male commuters (male weekday rides over 8 min).
cards.x: Each name comes from reading the OCT leaves, not from K-means itself.

cards.f: What does the fifth Blue Bikes cluster add?
cards.b: Long rides: rides over about 20 minutes (e.g. female > 23 min, male weekday > 18 min, male weekend > 21 min), split off from the commuter and weekend groups, which become medium-length rides.
cards.x: Raising K refines existing segments rather than reshuffling them.

cards.f: Why can one cluster appear in several OCT leaves?
cards.b: A cluster need not be a single axis-aligned box; the tree describes it as a union of leaves. E.g. with K=4, cluster 3 (short rides) covers female <4 min weekday, female <4 min weekend, male <8 min weekday and male <5 min weekend.
cards.x: Read a cluster as an OR of leaf rules.

o: Clustering uses no labels and segments data into similar groups
Clustering needs labels for only some points
Clustering predicts a continuous outcome
Clustering always produces exactly two groups
quiz.e: Clustering is unsupervised: data but no labels, with segmentation as the goal. Partly labeled data would be semi-supervised.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three factors the lecture says determine a clustering?
o: The size of the held-out test set
The distance metric
The partitioning algorithm
The criterion used to assess the solution
quiz.e: Metric, algorithm and quality criterion drive the partition. There is no test set in this unsupervised setting.

quiz.q: What is the Euclidean distance between $(1,2,3)$ and $(4,6,3)$?
quiz.e: $\sqrt{3^2+4^2+0^2} = 5$. 7 is Manhattan, 4 is Chebyshev and 25 forgets the square root.

quiz.q: What is the Chebyshev distance between $(1,2,3)$ and $(4,6,3)$?
quiz.e: Chebyshev is the largest absolute coordinate difference: $\max(3,4,0) = 4$. 7 is the Manhattan sum.

quiz.q: In the Minkowski family, which value of $p$ gives the Manhattan (city block) distance?
o: $p \to \infty$
quiz.e: $p=1$ sums absolute differences. $p=2$ is Euclidean; $p\to\infty$ is Chebyshev.

quiz.q: Points $(1,2)$, $(3,4)$ and $(5,0)$ are assigned to the same cluster. What is its K-means centroid?
quiz.e: Average each coordinate: $x = 9/3 = 3$, $y = 6/3 = 2$. $(9,6)$ is the sum, not the mean.

quiz.q: Centroids are $\mu_1 = (0,0)$ and $\mu_2 = (4,4)$ (Euclidean distance). In the assignment step, where does point $(3,2)$ go, and why?
o: Cluster 2: distance $\sqrt5 \approx 2.24$ vs $\sqrt{13} \approx 3.61$
Cluster 1: distance $\sqrt{13}$ vs $\sqrt5$
Cluster 1, because it is closer to the origin in the first coordinate
It is split equally between both clusters
quiz.e: $d((3,2),(0,0)) = \sqrt{9+4} = \sqrt{13}$; $d((3,2),(4,4)) = \sqrt{1+4} = \sqrt5$. K-means makes hard assignments to the nearest centroid.

quiz.q: Which of these is a partition (flat) clustering algorithm?
o: Mixture of Gaussians
Bottom-up agglomerative clustering
Top-down divisive clustering
Optimal Classification Trees
quiz.e: K-means, mixture of Gaussians and spectral clustering are partition algorithms. Agglomerative and divisive are hierarchical; OCTs are classifiers.

quiz.q: 1D data $\{1, 2, 9, 10, 11\}$, K-means with K=2 and initial centroids $\mu_1 = 1$, $\mu_2 = 2$. What are the centroids at convergence?
o: 1 and 8
1.5 and 8
2 and 10
quiz.e: Assign: {1} and {2,9,10,11}, so centroids 1 and 8. Reassign: 2 is closer to 1, giving {1,2} and {9,10,11}, so centroids 1.5 and 10. Reassigning changes nothing, so stop. '1 and 8' stops after one update.

quiz.q: On a line, cluster A = {0, 1} and cluster B = {4, 7}. What is the complete-linkage distance between them?
quiz.e: Complete linkage takes the maximum pairwise distance: $|0-7| = 7$. 3 is single linkage (min, $|1-4|$) and 5 is average or centroid linkage.

quiz.q: Cluster A = {(0,0), (0,2)} and cluster B = {(3,0)} (Euclidean). What is the average-linkage distance?
o: About 3.30
About 3.16
About 3.61
quiz.e: Pairwise distances are 3 and $\sqrt{13} \approx 3.61$, with mean $\approx 3.30$. 3.16 is centroid linkage ($(0,1)$ to $(3,0)$ is $\sqrt{10}$), 3 is single and 3.61 is complete.

quiz.q: In a dendrogram, what does the height of a vertical line represent?
o: The distance between the clusters being merged
The number of points in the cluster
The order in which points were read in
The cluster's centroid value
quiz.e: Heights encode merge distances; cutting horizontally at some height picks the number of clusters.

quiz.q: Which comparison of K-means and hierarchical clustering matches the lecture?
o: Hierarchical is deterministic but more computationally intensive; K-means uses little memory but depends on initialization
K-means is deterministic; hierarchical depends on random initialization
Hierarchical requires K in advance; K-means does not
Both produce interpretable, feature-based descriptions of clusters
quiz.e: K-means: low memory, init-sensitive, K fixed. Hierarchical: costlier, deterministic, dendrogram for many K. Neither is interpretable, which motivates the OCT step.

quiz.q: What is the lecture's recipe for interpretable clustering?
o: Run K-means, label each point with its cluster, then train an OCT with K classes
Train an OCT on the raw data with no labels
Run hierarchical clustering and report the dendrogram
Run K-means and report the centroids
quiz.e: The OCT is trained on the K-means labels, so its splits describe the clusters with features. Centroids alone do not give feature rules.

quiz.q: Why fit an OCT to K-means labels instead of simply reporting the K-means centroids?
o: Centroids don't give a set of features that characterizes each cluster; the tree gives explicit split rules
The OCT changes the cluster assignments to make them more accurate
K-means cannot assign new points without a tree
The OCT removes the need to choose K
quiz.e: The lecture's complaint is that clustering output is not interpretable: users cannot characterize a partition with features. The tree's splits (e.g. duration < 8, male, weekday) do that. K is still chosen by the user.

quiz.q: Which three variables describe each ride in the Blue Bikes case study?
o: Ride duration, rider gender, day of week
Start station, end station, duration
Rider age, gender, membership type
Time of day, weather, duration
quiz.e: The 2011 Hubway data with 79,593 rides use duration (minutes), gender and day of week (1-7).

quiz.q: In the K=4 Blue Bikes table, cluster 2 has leaves 'F, > 4 min, weekend' (3,449 rides) and 'M, 5-281 min, weekend' (7,570 rides). How many rides are in cluster 2?
quiz.e: $3{,}449 + 7{,}570 = 11{,}019$; a cluster's size is the sum over all leaves assigned to it. 13,152 is cluster 1.

quiz.q: In the K=4 Blue Bikes OCT, cluster 3 ('short rides') appears in four different leaves. What does this show?
o: A cluster can be described as a union of several tree leaves (an OR of rules)
The OCT failed to separate the clusters
K-means put the same rides in several clusters
The tree should be pruned until each cluster has one leaf
quiz.e: Short rides cover F < 4 weekday, F < 4 weekend, M < 8 weekday and M < 5 weekend: different thresholds by gender and day. One box cannot express that, so several leaves share a label; this is not an error.

written.q: A bike-share operator wants rider segments it can act on, using ride duration, rider gender and day of week. (a) Propose an interpretable clustering pipeline and justify each step. (b) Discuss the choices that will change the result (metric, algorithm, K) and how K-means and hierarchical clustering compare here. (c) Using the lecture's Blue Bikes results, describe the segments you would expect for K = 4 and what K = 5 adds.
written.m: (a) Prepare the three features (duration in minutes, gender, day of week). Run K-means for a chosen K: assign each ride to the nearest centroid and recompute centroids until no change. Label each ride with its cluster, then train an Optimal Classification Tree with K classes on the original features. The tree's splits (e.g. duration < 8, gender, weekday/weekend) characterize each cluster, which K-means alone cannot do. (b) With no ground truth, the partition depends on the distance metric (Euclidean, Manhattan, Chebyshev), the algorithm and the quality criterion. K-means is light on memory but sensitive to random initialization and needs K in advance; hierarchical clustering is deterministic and its dendrogram shows partitions for every K, but costs more computation (heavy for 79,593 rides) and needs a linkage choice. Neither is interpretable on its own. Try several K and keep the one whose tree gives the most useful segments. (c) K = 4: female commuters (female weekday rides over 4 min), weekend riders (weekend rides over 4-5 min), short rides (under 4-8 min) and male commuters (male weekday rides over 8 min). K = 5 splits off long rides (over about 20 minutes), turning the commuter and weekend groups into medium-length rides. A cluster can be the union of several leaves.
k: K-means, label, OCT with K classes, in that order
Why: OCT splits give feature-based cluster descriptions
Metric, algorithm and criterion drive the partition; no ground truth
K-means vs hierarchical trade-offs (memory, initialization, determinism, choice of K)
Correct K=4 segments from Blue Bikes
K=5 adds long rides; clusters as unions of leaves

written.q: Points on a line: 0, 2, 3, 7, 12. (a) Run agglomerative clustering with single linkage and list each merge with its height. (b) Repeat with complete linkage. (c) Cut each dendrogram to give K = 2 clusters and compare the results.
written.m: (a) Single linkage (minimum pairwise distance): merge {2,3} at 1; then {0} with {2,3} at $|0-2| = 2$; then {0,2,3} with {7} at $|7-3| = 4$ (less than $|12-7| = 5$); finally with {12} at 5. (b) Complete linkage (maximum pairwise distance): merge {2,3} at 1; then {0} with {2,3} at $\max(2,3) = 3$ (vs 5 for {2,3}-{7} and 5 for {7}-{12}); then {7} with {12} at 5 (vs 7 for {0,2,3}-{7}); finally {0,2,3} with {7,12} at $|12-0| = 12$. (c) Single linkage with K=2: {0,2,3,7} and {12}. Complete linkage with K=2: {0,2,3} and {7,12}. The linkage choice changes the partition: single linkage attaches 7 to the left group through its nearest point 3, while complete linkage weighs the far point 0 and pairs 7 with 12. This shows how the distance between clusters, not just between points, drives hierarchical clustering.
k: Correct single-linkage merge order and heights (1, 2, 4, 5)
Correct complete-linkage merge order and heights (1, 3, 5, 12)
Explains difference via min vs max pairwise distance
